claims.text: The unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy has a large caloric response but poor mechanical integrity and a tendency to crack.
Introducing 5–10 vol% uniformly dispersed SiC nanoparticles by powder processing and consolidation will form a reinforced composite.
SiC nanoparticles will arrest crack propagation in the alloy matrix.
SiC reinforcement will increase the compressive strength of the alloy.
A 5–10 vol% SiC addition will not significantly interfere with the caloric phase transition.
Homogeneously distributed SiC nanoparticles will deflect and blunt advancing cracks.
The nanoparticle–matrix interfaces will mediate stress transfer.
Crack deflection and bridging by the ceramic nanoparticles will toughen the composite.
SiC is non-magnetic and has high stiffness.
The non-magnetic and high-stiffness nature of SiC will preserve the intrinsic first-order caloric transition by avoiding disruption of the matrix's magnetic and structural interactions.
The reinforced composite should achieve a compressive-strength improvement comparable to or greater than the cited 152 MPa benchmark.
The reinforced composite should retain a caloric response of similar magnitude to that of the unmodified alloy.
The reinforced composite should exhibit fewer and less severe cracks during cyclic field and mechanical loading.
The beneficial balance of integrity and caloric response is expected only at approximately 5–10 vol% nanoparticle loading.
Nanoparticle loadings above the proposed range may hinder the caloric transition.
Nanoparticle loadings below the proposed range may be insufficient to improve mechanical properties.
Dispersion quality and interface characteristics may alter the kinetics of the caloric phase transition.
Processing parameters may affect nanoparticle distribution and thereby the balance between mechanical and caloric performance.
